Because EGFR-directed therapy produces prolonged control in advanced disease, extending it to the postoperative setting is a natural step, but the rationale is not identical: in advanced disease the target is bulk tumor, while after resection the target is an unobservable residual population whose existence can only be inferred. Perioperative strategies built on releasing the brakes that tumors place on cytotoxic T cells, which have changed practice for other genotypes, produce little benefit in this one, leaving receptor-directed therapy as the only rational option. Two questions therefore arise. Does treatment improve outcomes, and can the patients who need it be identified rather than treated indiscriminately for three years. Mechanistic work in advanced disease has established that escape is heterogeneous and often untreatable once established, which argues for intervening when the residual population is smallest.

sections.name: Methods
sections.text: Patients with completely removed stage IB to IIIA disease harboring exon 19 deletions or L858R, with or without prior adjuvant chemotherapy, were assigned 1:1 with stratification by stage, mutation type, and race. Treatment continued for three years or until recurrence. The primary endpoint was disease-free survival in stage II to IIIA by investigator assessment; 682 patients provided 80 percent power to detect a hazard ratio of 0.70 with 247 events. Imaging including brain magnetic resonance imaging was performed every 12 weeks for two years then every 24 weeks. In the substudy, blood was collected at 4 weeks after surgery and every 12 weeks, and assayed with a tumor-informed 16-target panel with a detection limit near 0.01 percent.

sections.name: Results
sections.text: Between 2015 and 2019, 339 patients received osimertinib and 343 placebo. At the interim analysis, with median follow-up 22 months, disease-free survival events had occurred in 37 versus 159 patients. In stage II to IIIA the hazard ratio was 0.17, and in the overall population 0.20. Two-year disease-free survival was 89 versus 53 percent. Recurrence involving the central nervous system occurred in 6 versus 39 patients. In the substudy, postoperative tumor DNA was detected in 61 of 288 patients; recurrence occurred in 34 of these versus 29 of 227 without detection, hazard ratio 5.4. Among patients with detectable DNA, disease-free survival hazard ratio for treatment was 0.11 versus 0.31 for those without. Grade 3 or higher events occurred in 20 versus 13 percent, and 11 percent discontinued treatment for adverse events.

sections.name: Discussion
sections.text: Three years of postoperative EGFR-directed therapy markedly delays recurrence, with the largest absolute benefit in higher-stage disease and a striking reduction in recurrence within the central nervous system. The residual disease substudy suggests a path away from treating everyone: detectable tumor DNA at four weeks after surgery identifies a group with a five-fold higher recurrence risk and the greatest benefit from treatment, while the majority without detection have a favorable outcome that may not justify three years of therapy and its costs. Overall survival data are immature and the trial cannot yet establish whether delayed recurrence translates into cure or into deferred relapse. A related concern is that patients who recur after adjuvant exposure enter the advanced setting having already been selected by the drug, and the spectrum of escape in that population is unknown.

title: Prophylactic management of dermatologic and infusion reactions with amivantamab plus lazertinib: a randomized supportive care study

sections.name: Abstract
sections.text: Combined receptor-directed antibody and third-generation inhibitor therapy produces high rates of rash, paronychia, and first-infusion reactions that lead to dose interruption in a third of patients and compromise delivery of an active regimen. We randomized 244 patients starting amivantamab plus lazertinib to a structured prophylaxis package, comprising oral doxycycline, topical clindamycin, chlorhexidine nail soaks, and antihistamine plus corticosteroid premedication with split first dosing, or to reactive management. The primary endpoint, grade 2 or higher dermatologic events within 12 weeks, occurred in 38 percent with prophylaxis versus 76 percent with reactive management, absolute difference 38 percentage points. Infusion reactions occurred in 41 versus 67 percent. Dose interruption for any reason occurred in 19 versus 44 percent, and relative dose intensity at 12 weeks was 94 versus 81 percent. Response rates did not differ.

sections.name: Introduction
sections.text: Regimens that engage the wild-type receptor in skin and gut are limited less by efficacy than by tolerability, and the resulting interruptions reduce delivered dose at exactly the time when disease control is being established. This is not a cosmetic issue: paronychia can prevent walking, and severe acneiform eruption is a common reason for patients to stop an effective drug. The registrational trial of the antibody reported infusion-related reactions in about two thirds of patients, almost entirely with the first infusion, and rash in the great majority, which established the scale of the problem but not how to manage it. Prophylaxis packages have been evaluated for single-agent inhibitors but not for the antibody-inhibitor pair, where the mechanisms of skin injury are additive.

sections.name: Methods
sections.text: Patients starting amivantamab plus lazertinib for EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma were randomized 1:1, stratified by prior therapy and by sex. The prophylaxis arm received doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 12 weeks, topical clindamycin, chlorhexidine 0.1 percent nail soaks three times weekly, non-comedogenic emollient, and premedication with dexamethasone, diphenhydramine, and acetaminophen with the first dose split across two days. The reactive arm received the same agents only after events occurred. The primary endpoint was grade 2 or higher dermatologic events within 12 weeks by CTCAE version 5.0, assessed by a dermatologist blinded to assignment; 244 patients provided 90 percent power to detect a 20 percentage point difference. Relative dose intensity and patient-reported skin-specific quality of life were secondary.

sections.name: Results
sections.text: Between 2022 and 2023, 122 patients were assigned to each arm. Grade 2 or higher dermatologic events within 12 weeks occurred in 46 versus 93 patients, 38 versus 76 percent, risk difference 38 percentage points with 95 percent confidence interval 27 to 49. Grade 3 events occurred in 6 versus 21 patients. Paronychia of any grade occurred in 31 versus 58 percent. First-infusion reactions occurred in 50 versus 82 patients, and reactions with subsequent infusions were rare in both arms. Dose interruption occurred in 23 versus 54 patients and permanent discontinuation for these events in 4 versus 12. Relative dose intensity at 12 weeks was 94 versus 81 percent. Skin-specific quality of life scores favored prophylaxis at every timepoint. Objective response rates were 63 and 60 percent, and doxycycline-related photosensitivity occurred in 9 patients.

sections.name: Discussion
sections.text: Structured prophylaxis halves clinically significant skin events and substantially reduces interruptions, with no evidence that suppressing the rash compromises antitumor activity, a concern that has circulated since rash was observed to correlate with benefit for earlier agents. The effect on delivered dose is the most consequential result, since regimens of this class are given for years and cumulative dose is likely to matter. Practically, prophylaxis should begin on day 1 rather than at first event, and nail care should be included, since paronychia emerges later than rash and is the more common reason for interruption after week 8. Limitations include the open-label design for patients and treating physicians, the single regimen studied, and follow-up limited to 12 weeks, which cannot address late or cumulative effects.
